report:
## Research Findings: Olive Leaf Extract and Blood Pressure

The evidence does not support a firm "no" — several controlled trials and pooled analyses suggest olive leaf extract (OLE) can modestly lower blood pressure, though the evidence base is limited and of low-to-moderate quality.

**Key studies:**
- A landmark double-blind RCT (Susalit et al., 2011, *Phytomedicine*) compared OLE (EFLA®943, standardized oleuropein extract) to the ACE-inhibitor captopril in stage-1 hypertensive patients over 8 weeks. OLE produced blood pressure reductions comparable to captopril (https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2011/03/09/Olive-leaf-extract-may-help-hypertension-Frutarom-study/).
- A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis (published in *BMC Diabetology & Metabolic Syndrome*) pooling multiple RCTs found OLE supplementation significantly reduced several cardiovascular risk markers, including blood pressure, alongside lipid and inflammatory improvements (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y).
- A related meta-analysis (2022, cited via ResearchGate) reported a standardized systolic BP reduction across studies of borderline-to-moderate significance (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/361409918_The_effect_of_olive_leaf_use_on_blood_pressure_A_systematic_review_and_meta-analysis).
- However, an independent evidence summary (Examine.com) reviewing 3 RCTs (n=248) concluded OLE reduced systolic BP compared to baseline, but **not significantly versus placebo/no-treatment control** — highlighting that much of the apparent effect may reflect natural fluctuation rather than a true drug-like effect (https://examine.com/research-feed/study/0qyQG0/).

**Conclusion:** The current evidence is mixed and preliminary rather than conclusively negative. Small trials suggest a modest antihypertensive effect, particularly in people with mild/borderline hypertension, but larger, more rigorous placebo-controlled trials are needed before olive leaf extract can be considered a reliably effective treatment. Thus, "no effect at all" overstates the case — a more accurate answer is "possibly a small effect, but evidence remains inconclusive."
